newsitem.title: KENYA: Aid agencies say Somali leaders must fight drought.
newsitem.headline: Aid agencies say Somali leaders must fight drought.

text.p: Aid agencies said on Wednesday Somalia's faction leaders are primarily responsible for fighting the drought there and should improve security to allow foreign aid workers to operate.
Answering a flood of recent appeals from faction leaders for international aid to drought-stricken Somalia, the Somali Aid Coordination Body (SACB) said Somalis were not doing enough themselves.

"The SACB wishes to stress that an appropriate response to the effect of the current drought cannot come solely from the international community," said the Nairobi-based body, which groups foreign donors and aid agencies operating in Somalia.
"Primary responsibility to respond to the distress of the most vulnerable members of the Somali population rests with the Somali leaders," it said in a rare public rebuke of the chiefs.

A day after telling aid agencies to move to recognise his state or leave, President Mohamed Ibrahim Egal of self-declared Somaliland in northwest Somalia declared his region on Wednesday drought-stricken and appealed for international help.

South Mogadishu-based faction leader Hussein Aideed, elected president of Somalia by supporters last August, told Reuters this week he expected the international community to help and he would give security to aid workers at his ports and airports.
Faction leaders say the situation in much of Somalia is reminiscent of 1992, when 300,000 people were killed by famine fuelled by civil war. Aid officials said they are exaggerating.

"The international aid community can only react to the current drought conditions...if the necessary measures are taken by the Somali population," said the SACB one day after talks between aid officials and Aideed in the Kenyan capital Nairobi.
"The onus for ensuring freedom of access to affected areas, guaranteeing the security of aid personnel and allowing the free movement of goods rests wholly with the Somali people and their leaders.

"And only the Somali people and their leaders have the authority and responsibility of ensuring that existing infrastructure, such as air and sea ports, is made available to the international community," the SACB said in a statement.

"The Somali leaders also bear the responsibility and the moral obligation to promote reconciliation and peace, without which no lasting solution to the fundamental problems of the Somali population will be possible," the statement added.
The U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation said in a report on Wednesday the secondary "Der" crop in Somalia, which accounts for 25 percent of annual cereal production, was 60 percent below 1995/96.
It said donors should make contingency plans to send food.
All international aid workers pulled out of the Aideed fiefdom of southern Mogadishu shortly before the withdrawal of the last U.N. peacekeepers from Somalia in March 1995.
Gunmen have abducted more than a dozen foreign aid workers in parts of Somalia in the last few years, mainly for ransom.

Hussein Aideed is a 34-year-old former U.S. marine who briefly served with U.S. forces which landed in Mogadishu in December 1992 at the start of Operation Restore Hope to protect aid agency convoys from marauding gunmen during the famine.

Aideed said this week if long rains later this month failed, drought would be a huge problem in much of Somalia but he would give unrestricted access to aid agencies to areas in and outside this control.
Aideed blasted a peace pact in January after weeks of talks in Ethiopia among 26 faction leaders opposed to his claim to the presidency as foreign manipulation. He boycotted the talks.
